topic: Sentence Completion (Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension)

sections.title: Level 2 Sentence Completion Concept
sections.content: At Level 2, sentences become more formal and complex, often related to economics, editorials, or policy discussions. The first part of the sentence is given and a blank appears at the end. The options usually contain longer clauses that must match the tone, tense, and structure of the sentence.

sections.title: Logical Continuation in Formal Context
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the topic of the sentence (such as economy, policy, or governance). Step 2: Understand the main idea of the first part. Step 3: Choose a clause that logically continues the idea in the same formal tone.

sections.title: Parallel Structure Check
sections.content: Step 1: If the sentence includes a list or multiple actions, examine their grammatical form. Step 2: The option must maintain the same pattern. Step 3: For example, if the first part says 'improving efficiency and reducing costs', the continuation should maintain the same structural balance.

sections.title: Tense Consistency
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the tense used in the main clause. Step 2: Check whether the option matches the same time reference. Step 3: If the sentence is discussing a present policy situation, a past-tense continuation may be incorrect.

sections.title: Editorial Tone Recognition
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the tone of the sentence (formal, analytical, neutral). Step 2: The option must also follow the same editorial style. Step 3: Eliminate options that sound overly informal or conversational.

sections.title: Trap Identification
sections.content: Step 1: Some options may appear logically correct. Step 2: However, they may contain tense mismatches, parallelism errors, or tone inconsistencies. Step 3: Eliminate these traps by carefully checking grammar and structure.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: At Level 2, both meaning and grammar must be evaluated carefully. The correct answer will provide a logical continuation, maintain tense consistency, and preserve the editorial tone of the sentence.

tricks.title: Topic Recognition Trick
tricks.explanation: First identify whether the sentence relates to economy, policy, or governance.
tricks.example: The government introduced new fiscal reforms to strengthen the economy, __________.

tricks.title: Grammar Before Meaning
tricks.explanation: Immediately eliminate options that are grammatically incorrect, even if they seem meaningful.
tricks.example: An option may sound logical but becomes incorrect due to tense mismatch.

tricks.title: Parallel Structure Check
tricks.explanation: If the sentence includes two actions, both should follow the same grammatical form.
tricks.example: The policy aims at improving transparency and reducing corruption.

tricks.title: Tense Alignment Trick
tricks.explanation: Choose the continuation according to the tense used in the main clause.
tricks.example: If the sentence is written in present analysis, avoid past-tense continuations.

tricks.title: Editorial Tone Filter
tricks.explanation: Eliminate options that sound informal or conversational.
tricks.example: Formal analysis should avoid casual expressions.

tricks.title: Logical Policy Outcome
tricks.explanation: In policy-related sentences, the continuation often describes the impact or implication.
tricks.example: The reform was designed to improve public spending efficiency.

tricks.title: Elimination Method
tricks.explanation: First eliminate two options based on grammar or tone.
tricks.example: Then it becomes easier to choose the logical continuation from the remaining options.

tricks.title: Clause Length Balance
tricks.explanation: The length and complexity of the continuation clause should match the first part of the sentence.
tricks.example: Formal sentences often continue with structured analytical clauses.
